Award/Judgment Factual Position And Pleadings
1. This Dar was filed on 10.07.2013 by the Investigating Officer in the presence of all the parties.
The Dar is related to a motor vehicular accident dated 11.06.2013 i

n which one Sh. Murari @
Murari Shrivastav S/o Sh. Om Prakash (hereinafter referred to as "petitioner") sustained grievous injuries.

As per DAR, on 11.06.2013 at about 09.30 P.M., the petitioner was riding his bicycle to his home situated at Sangam Vihar, Burari, Delhi and when he reached at a spot situated opposite Indian Clinic on the Main Road, Burari Garhi Village, Delhi he was hit in the rear by a motorcycle bearing registration number DL-8SAZ-6992 (hereinafter referred to as "offending vehicle").
Petitioner fell down, sustained grievous injuries and was immediately removed to Trauma Centre by a PCR vehicle.

An FIR no. 229/13 PS Burari was registered by the police U/s 279/337 IPC on its own on the basis of DD No. 48A dated 11.06.2013, recorded in the PS with respect to above accident,
after considering the materials available at the spot and the MLC of the petitioner.
During the course of investigation police was able to trace out the driver and owner of the offending vehicle.

R-1 is stated to be the rider of the offending vehicle.
R-2 is stated to be the owner of the offending vehicle and R-3 is stated to be the insurer of the offending vehicle.
DAR was treated as a claim petition.

ISSUE NO.1 "Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in a road traffic accident dated 11/06/2013 due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle bearing No. DL 8SA2 6992 driven by respondent no. 1 as alleged?
9.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 LOVLEEN Date:
(Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs.
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.

sentences.text: In order to decide the present issue, we must delve into the oral testimonies of petitioner, who examined himself as PW-1 and R-1,who examined himself as R1W1.
As per PW-1, the accident took place when his bicycle was hit in the rear by the offending vehicle which R-1 was riding at a high speed and in a rash and negligent manner.
As per R-1, no such accident, as deposed by PW-1, ever took place.
He claims that his motorcycle ( i.e. offending vehicle) was hit by some unknown motorcycle at the relevant time but the petitioner lost control over his bicycle, he fell down and sustained injuries.
As per R-1, the offending vehicle did not come in contact with the bicycle of PW-1.
10.1 Apparently, both the said parties have made contradictory claims as to the facts and circumstances surrounding the occurrence of the accident.

However, the oral testimony of R-1,
discussed above, is liable to be rejected summarily, being beyond the pleadings, as no written statement was filed by him or by R-2 in the present matter.
Even on merits, the claim of R-1 is liable to be rejected, being an after thought, as he failed to put his case to PW-1 during the course of cross examination.
On the other hand, the brief cross examination of PW-1 does not reveal any inconsistency.

During cross examination, PW-1 was able to depose about the time when he left his place of employment on the relevant date, the LOVLEEN Date:
Murari @ Murari Shrivastav vs Suraj on 19 January, 2023

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120704002/
6 distance between his place of employment and scene of occurrence and also the direction from which the offending vehicle hit his bicycle at the relevant time.
PW-1 declined all the suggestions challenging his testimony as to the facts and circumstances surrounding the occurrence of the accident.

PW-1 seems to have withstood the test of cross examination as the respondents could not bring any material on record which reflects any falsity or untruth in the oral testimony of PW-1.
11.

The very fact that R-1 has already been charge- sheeted for the offences punishable under Sections 279/338 IPC and Section 3/181 of M.V Act in the above criminal case/FIR in itself is a strong circumstance to support the above oral testimony of PW1 and the case of petitioner on this issue.

The copies of FIR, Charge-sheet, Mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle, MLC,
Seizure Memo and Arrest Memo of R- 1 also corroborate the oral testimony of PW1.
12. In view of the above, it could be safely assumed that the offending vehicle hit petitioner's bicycle in the rear at the relevant time.

13. Having ruled so, this Tribunal now proceeds to assess the wrongful act, neglect or default of R-1,
if any, in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending vehicle) hit the petitioner's bicycle in the rear at the relevant time.

In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any LOVLEEN Date:
material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the petitioner,
the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in riding the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
In view of the above discussion, this Tribunal is constrained to hold R-1 guilty of gross neglect and default in riding the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
14. In view of the medical treatment documents placed on record by the petitioner, no dispute is left regarding the nature of injuries sustained by him in the above accident.

15. In view of the above discussion, this Tribunal holds that the petitioner suffered grievous injuries on his person on account of neglect and default of R-1 while riding the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
This issue thus stands decided against the respondents and in favour of the petitioner.
"Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?

If so, to what amount and from whom?"
16.

As the issue no.1 has been proved in affirmative and in favour of the petitioner, the petitioner has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered in the above accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.

In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.

The pecuniary damages or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by him in the accident.
The non-pecuniary or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc.
and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.

It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate him or to put him almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The object of compensating him is also not to reward him or to make him rich Digitally signed by LOVLEEN LOVLEEN Date:
2023.01.19 16:55:05 +0530 in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled

that the 'just'
compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.

Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1995 SC 755, Arvind Kumar Mishra Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited, (2010) 10 SCC 254 and Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343.

In his affidavit Ex. PW1/A, the petitioner states that at the relevant time he was employed at M/s Swastik Stationary Products, Burari, Delhi and was earning Rs. 14,000/- per month from his employment but his life has turned gloomy after the accident on account of impairment of bodily integrity.
It was argued by the Ld. Counsel for the petitioner that since the occurrence of the accident the petitioner could not resume his employment on account of injuries sustained in the accident.
He further argued that the petitioner has sustained 100% functional disability due to the accident.

He relied upon the medical records Ex. PW1/2 and the medical examination reports Ex.
PW2/A and Ex. PW2/B to buttress his arguments.

21.1 A bare perusal of the discharge summary Ex. PW1/2 reflects that the petitioner sustained 'Rt Frontotemporal Acute SDH with Temporal Contusion with L-sided Temporal Contusion' and underwent 'Rt-Sided Decompression Hemi Craniotomy & Placement of Bone Flap in anterior abdominal wall on 12.06.2013'.
As per medical examination report Ex. PW2/A '' Mr. Murari Lal Shrivastava is a case of alleged head injury following RTA on 12/06/2013.
He underwent right sided decompressive hemicraniotomy on the same day.
Detailed neuropsychiatric evaluation revealed cognitive decline ( MMSE- 14/29), visuospatial disorientation, minimal left UMN facial palsy with normal tone, power and reflexes.
On neuropsychological assessment on PGI-BBD patient is having significant cognitive dysfunction''.

During the course of present proceedings PW-2 Dr. Jyoti Garg clarified that Significant LOVLEEN Date:
Cognitive Dysfunction means patient is unable to do his daily activities by himself independently and he would need constant assistance of others for his daily activities.
In totality, the above facts are sufficient to presume that the petitioner has sustained 100% functional disability.
21.2 It may be noted here that petitioner has failed to place any material on record in order to corroborate his claim as to his vocation/ employment or his income at the relevant time.

In the absence of any material as to the monthly earnings of the petitioner, it would be appropriate to assume the monthly earnings of the petitioner as per the minimum wages payable to an unskilled person in Delhi ( petitioner being an ordinary resident of Delhi) as on the date of accident.
As per relevant notification, the minimum wages admissible to an unskilled person as on 11/06/2013 in Delhi were Rs. 7,722/-.

Accordingly, the monthly income of petitioner is assumed to be Rs. 7,722/.
As far as the age of petitioner at the time of accident is concerned, we may rely on PAN Card Ex.
PW1/5, placed on record by petitioner, as per which document his date of birth is 21.05.1967.
As per said document, the petitioner was aged about 46 years as on the date of accident i.e. 11/06/2013.
Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma & Ors.

2. What amount of compensation the petitioner is entitled to and from whom?
I have perused the record and my issue wise findings is as under:-
ISSUE NO.1 "Whether the petitioner suffered injuries in a road traffic accident dated 11/06/2013 due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle bearing No. DL 8SA2 6992 driven by respondent no. 1 as alleged?
9.
15. In view of the above discussion, this Tribunal holds that the petitioner suffered grievous injuries on his person on account of neglect and default of R-1 while riding the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
"Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
If so, to what amount and from whom?"

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 LOVLEEN Date:
(Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs.
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
10.
Even on merits, the claim of R-1 is liable to be rejected, being an after thought, as he failed to put his case to PW-1 during the course of cross examination.
PW-1 declined all the suggestions challenging his testimony as to the facts and circumstances surrounding the occurrence of the accident.
PW-1 seems to have withstood the test of cross examination as the respondents could not bring any material on record which reflects any falsity or untruth in the oral testimony of PW-1.
11.
12. In view of the above, it could be safely assumed that the offending vehicle hit petitioner's bicycle in the rear at the relevant time.
13. Having ruled so, this Tribunal now proceeds to assess the wrongful act, neglect or default of R-1,
if any, in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending vehicle) hit the petitioner's bicycle in the rear at the relevant time.
In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any LOVLEEN Date:
material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the petitioner,
the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in riding the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
As the issue no.1 has been proved in affirmative and in favour of the petitioner, the petitioner has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered in the above accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.
The pecuniary damages or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by him in the accident.
The non-pecuniary or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.
The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc.
and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate him or to put him almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating him is also not to reward him or to make him rich Digitally signed by LOVLEEN LOVLEEN Date:
2023.01.19 16:55:05 +0530 in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled
that the 'just'
compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.
Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1995 SC 755, Arvind Kumar Mishra Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited, (2010) 10 SCC 254 and Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343.
18.
In the absence of any material as to the monthly earnings of the petitioner, it would be appropriate to assume the monthly earnings of the petitioner as per the minimum wages payable to an unskilled person in Delhi ( petitioner being an ordinary resident of Delhi) as on the date of accident.
As per relevant notification, the minimum wages admissible to an unskilled person as on 11/06/2013 in Delhi were Rs. 7,722/-.
Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma & Ors.
9 Vs. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr., (2009) 6 SCC 121, which has also been upheld by the Constitution Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a recent judgment dated 31.10.2017 given in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.
